blocks.body:
Pick up a square and put it back so that it covers exactly the same region. There are eight ways to do it: four rotations (by $0^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$, $270^\circ$) and four reflections (in the two diagonals and in the two lines joining midpoints of opposite sides). Doing one of these motions and then another is again one of them, each can be undone, and doing nothing is one of them. A group is what remains when you keep these three features and forget the square.

The reward for abstracting is that one argument then covers rotations, permutations, numbers modulo $n$ and invertible matrices at once. This page builds the definition and proves the first two tools: Lagrange's theorem (the size of a subgroup divides the size of the group, which contains Fermat's little theorem as a special case) and Burnside's lemma (a formula for counting objects up to symmetry, such as colourings of a cube).

blocks.title: Symmetries compose, and order matters
blocks.body:
Number the corners of the square $1,2,3,4$ going anticlockwise. A symmetry moves corners to corners, so it can be recorded as a permutation of $\{1,2,3,4\}$. Let $r$ be the anticlockwise rotation by $90^\circ$, so $r$ sends $1\to2\to3\to4\to1$, and let $s$ be the reflection in the diagonal through corners $1$ and $3$, so $s$ fixes $1$ and $3$ and swaps $2$ and $4$.

Write $rs$ for "first do $s$, then do $r$" (the usual convention for composing functions). Then $rs$ sends corner $1$ to $r(s(1)) = r(1) = 2$, while $sr$ sends $1$ to $s(r(1)) = s(2) = 4$. So $rs \ne sr$: working out all four corners, $rs$ swaps $1\leftrightarrow2$ and $3\leftrightarrow4$ (a reflection in a line through edge midpoints), while $sr$ swaps $1\leftrightarrow4$ and $2\leftrightarrow3$ (the other such reflection).

Three facts are visible already. Composition of symmetries is associative, because composition of functions always is. There is an identity motion. Every motion has an inverse. Commutativity, on the other hand, fails, and the theory has to live without it.

blocks.title: Group
Examples, non-examples and first consequences
blocks.body:
Examples to keep in mind:

- $(\mathbb Z, +)$: the identity is $0$ and the inverse of $a$ is $-a$. Abelian and infinite.
- $\mathbb Z/n$, the residues $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ under addition modulo $n$ ([[congruences]]). Abelian, order $n$.
- $(\mathbb Z/p)^\times$ for a prime $p$: the nonzero residues $1, \dots, p-1$ under multiplication modulo $p$. Inverses exist because every $a$ with $p \nmid a$ has a [[mod-inverse|modular inverse]]. Order $p-1$. More generally $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$, the residues coprime to $n$, is a group of order $\varphi(n)$ ([[arithmetic-functions]]).
- $S_n$, all permutations of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ under composition. Order $n!$; not abelian once $n \ge 3$.
- $D_n$, the symmetries of a regular $n$-gon: $n$ rotations and $n$ reflections, order $2n$. The square group above is $D_4$.
- The invertible $2\times 2$ real matrices under matrix multiplication.

Non-examples: $(\mathbb N, +)$ has no inverses; the integers under multiplication have no inverse for $2$; and $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ under multiplication modulo $6$ is not even closed, since $2 \cdot 3 \equiv 0 \pmod 6$.

A few rules follow at once from the axioms. The identity is unique: if $e$ and $e'$ both work then $e = ee' = e'$. Inverses are unique, and we may cancel: if $ab = ac$ then multiplying on the left by $a^{-1}$ gives $b = c$. Also $(ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}$ (undo the last action first), since $(ab)(b^{-1}a^{-1}) = a(bb^{-1})a^{-1} = e$. Powers are defined as usual: $g^0 = e$, $g^{n+1} = g^n g$, and $g^{-n} = (g^{-1})^n$.

blocks.title: Subgroup and order of an element
blocks.body:
A subset $H \subseteq G$ is a subgroup if it contains $e$ and is closed under the operation and under taking inverses; $H$ is then a group in its own right. The order $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ of an element $g$ is the least $n \ge 1$ with $g^n = e$, if such an $n$ exists.

If $\operatorname{ord}(g) = n$, the powers $e, g, \dots, g^{n-1}$ are distinct (if $g^i = g^j$ with $0 \le i < j < n$ then $g^{j-i} = e$ with $0 < j-i < n$), and they form a subgroup $\langle g \rangle$ with exactly $n$ elements, since $g^n = e$ makes the powers wrap around and $g^{n-i}$ is the inverse of $g^i$. In a finite group every element has finite order, because the powers of $g$ cannot all be different.

blocks.title: Cosets: slicing a group into equal pieces
blocks.body:
Take $G = \mathbb Z/12$ (written additively) and the subgroup $H = \{0, 4, 8\}$. Shifting $H$ by each element gives only four different sets:

$$\{0,4,8\},\quad \{1,5,9\},\quad \{2,6,10\},\quad \{3,7,11\}.$$

They do not overlap, they cover $G$, and each has $3$ elements, so $12 = 4 \cdot 3$. That is Lagrange's theorem in miniature.

In general, for a subgroup $H$ of $G$ and an element $g$, the left coset of $H$ through $g$ is $gH = \{gh : h \in H\}$. In additive notation it is $g + H$.

blocks.title: Lagrange's theorem
blocks.body:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $H$ a subgroup. Then the distinct left cosets of $H$ partition $G$ and each has exactly $|H|$ elements. Hence

$$|G| = [G:H]\cdot|H|,$$

where the index $[G:H]$ is the number of left cosets. In particular $|H|$ divides $|G|$.

We check three facts.

1. Every $g \in G$ lies in some coset, namely $g = ge \in gH$.
2. Every coset has $|H|$ elements: the map $h \mapsto gh$ from $H$ to $gH$ is onto by the definition of $gH$, and one-to-one by cancellation ($gh_1 = gh_2$ implies $h_1 = h_2$).
3. Two cosets are either equal or disjoint. Suppose $x \in aH \cap bH$, say $x = ah_1 = bh_2$ with $h_1, h_2 \in H$. Then $a = bh_2h_1^{-1}$, so for every $h \in H$ we get $ah = b(h_2h_1^{-1}h)$, which lies in $bH$ because $H$ is closed under products and inverses. Thus $aH \subseteq bH$, and the same argument with $a$ and $b$ exchanged gives $bH \subseteq aH$.

So the distinct cosets cut $G$ into $[G:H]$ disjoint blocks of size $|H|$, and $|G| = [G:H]\,|H|$.
blocks.title: Proof of Lagrange's theorem
Consequences of Lagrange
blocks.body:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $g \in G$. Then $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ divides $|G|$, and $g^{|G|} = e$.

Taking $G = (\mathbb Z/p)^\times$ gives Fermat's little theorem: $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ whenever $p \nmid a$. Taking $G = (\mathbb Z/n)^\times$ gives Euler's theorem: $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ whenever $\gcd(a,n) = 1$.

The cyclic subgroup $\langle g \rangle$ has $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ elements, so by Lagrange $|G| = k \cdot \operatorname{ord}(g)$ for some integer $k$. Then $g^{|G|} = \big(g^{\operatorname{ord}(g)}\big)^k = e^k = e$. The two congruences are this statement read inside the groups $(\mathbb Z/p)^\times$, of order $p-1$, and $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$, of order $\varphi(n)$.

blocks.title: Groups acting on sets
blocks.body:
Groups usually arrive as symmetries of something: of a square, of the set of colourings of a necklace, of the roots of a polynomial. The general notion is an action.

An action of a group $G$ on a set $X$ assigns to each $g \in G$ and $x \in X$ an element $g\cdot x \in X$ such that $e \cdot x = x$ and $g\cdot(h\cdot x) = (gh)\cdot x$ for all $g, h, x$. For $x \in X$ and $g \in G$ define

- the orbit $\operatorname{Orb}(x) = \{g\cdot x : g \in G\}$, everywhere $x$ can be moved to;
- the stabiliser $\operatorname{Stab}(x) = \{g \in G : g\cdot x = x\}$, a subgroup of $G$;
- the fixed set $\operatorname{Fix}(g) = \{x \in X : g\cdot x = x\}$.

Two points are in the same orbit exactly when some group element moves one to the other; this is an equivalence relation (use $e$, inverses and composition), so the orbits partition $X$.

For the square group $D_4$ acting on the four corners there is a single orbit of size $4$, and the stabiliser of corner $1$ is $\{e, s\}$, of size $2$. Note that $4 \cdot 2 = 8 = |D_4|$. This is no accident.

blocks.title: Orbit–stabiliser theorem
blocks.body:
If a finite group $G$ acts on a set $X$, then for every $x \in X$

$$|\operatorname{Orb}(x)| \cdot |\operatorname{Stab}(x)| = |G|.$$

Write $S = \operatorname{Stab}(x)$. For $g, h \in G$,

$$g\cdot x = h\cdot x \iff (h^{-1}g)\cdot x = x \iff h^{-1}g \in S \iff g \in hS \iff gS = hS.$$

(For the first step apply $h^{-1}$ to both sides, or $h$ to go back; the last step uses fact 3 of the proof of Lagrange, because $g \in gS \cap hS$.) Hence the rule $g\cdot x \mapsto gS$ is a well-defined, one-to-one correspondence between the points of the orbit and the left cosets of $S$. There are $|G|/|S|$ cosets by Lagrange, so $|\operatorname{Orb}(x)| = |G|/|S|$.

blocks.title: Burnside's lemma
blocks.body:
If a finite group $G$ acts on a finite set $X$, the number of orbits is

$$\#\text{orbits} = \frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}|\operatorname{Fix}(g)|.$$

In words: the number of essentially different objects is the average number of objects fixed by a symmetry. (The formula was known to Cauchy and Frobenius before Burnside, and is also called the Cauchy–Frobenius lemma.)

Count the pairs $(g, x) \in G \times X$ with $g\cdot x = x$ in two ways. Grouping by $g$, the count is $\sum_{g} |\operatorname{Fix}(g)|$. Grouping by $x$, it is $\sum_{x} |\operatorname{Stab}(x)|$, which by orbit–stabiliser equals $\sum_{x} |G|/|\operatorname{Orb}(x)|$.

Now split this last sum by orbits. An orbit $O$ contributes $\sum_{x \in O} |G|/|O| = |G|$. So the total is $|G|$ times the number of orbits, and dividing by $|G|$ gives the formula.
blocks.title: Proof of Burnside's lemma
How Burnside is used for colourings
blocks.body:
Suppose the positions of an object (corners, beads, faces) are coloured with $k$ colours, and a symmetry group $G$ permutes the positions. Two colourings count as the same if a symmetry carries one to the other, so the essentially different colourings are the orbits of $G$ acting on the $k^{\text{positions}}$ colourings.

Write a symmetry $g$ as a product of disjoint cycles on the positions. A colouring is fixed by $g$ exactly when it is constant along each cycle, so

$$|\operatorname{Fix}(g)| = k^{c(g)},$$

where $c(g)$ is the number of cycles of $g$, fixed positions counting as cycles of length one. Elements of the same geometric type (for example, all rotations by $120^\circ$ about a long diagonal of a cube) have the same $c(g)$, so in practice one makes a short table of types, how many elements of each type there are, and their cycle counts.
Find the order of every element of $(\mathbb Z/7)^\times = \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ and check that each order divides $6$. Is the group generated by a single element?
blocks.solution:
List powers until $1$ appears.

- $1$: order $1$.
- $2$: $2, 4, 8 \equiv 1$, order $3$.
- $3$: $3, 9\equiv 2, 6, 18 \equiv 4, 12 \equiv 5, 15 \equiv 1$, order $6$.
- $4$: $4, 16\equiv 2, 8 \equiv 1$, order $3$.
- $5$: $5, 25 \equiv 4, 20 \equiv 6, 30 \equiv 2, 10 \equiv 3, 15 \equiv 1$, order $6$.
- $6$: $6, 36 \equiv 1$, order $2$.

The orders $1, 3, 6, 3, 6, 2$ all divide $|G| = 6$, as Lagrange requires. Since $3$ has order $6$, its powers exhaust the group, so the group is cyclic, generated by $3$ (and also by $5$). In the language of [[order-primroot]], $3$ and $5$ are the primitive roots modulo $7$. The subgroups are $\{1\}$, $\{1,6\}$, $\{1,2,4\}$ and the whole group, of orders $1, 2, 3, 6$.
blocks.title: Orders in the group modulo 7

blocks.body: Let $G$ be a group in which $g^2 = e$ for every element $g$. Prove that $G$ is abelian.
blocks.solution:
The condition $g^2 = e$ says $g = g^{-1}$ for every $g$. Take any $a, b \in G$. Applying this to $ab$, then the rule for the inverse of a product, then the condition to $a$ and $b$:

$$ab = (ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1} = ba.$$

So any two elements commute. (Example: $\mathbb Z/2 \times \mathbb Z/2$, the group of symmetries of a non-square rectangle.)
blocks.title: Squares to the identity

blocks.body: Each corner of a square is painted one of $3$ colours. How many essentially different colourings are there if two colourings are the same when (a) a rotation carries one to the other, (b) any symmetry of the square, rotation or reflection, carries one to the other?
blocks.solution:
There are $3^4 = 81$ colourings. Use $|\operatorname{Fix}(g)| = 3^{c(g)}$.

(a) The rotation group has $4$ elements. The identity has $4$ cycles (fixes $81$ colourings); the rotations by $90^\circ$ and $270^\circ$ are single $4$-cycles ($3$ each); the rotation by $180^\circ$ is $(1\,3)(2\,4)$, two cycles ($9$). Burnside gives

$$\frac{81 + 3 + 9 + 3}{4} = \frac{96}{4} = 24.$$

(b) Add the four reflections. A diagonal reflection fixes two corners and swaps the other two: $3$ cycles, $27$ colourings each. A reflection through edge midpoints consists of two $2$-cycles: $9$ each. Now

$$\frac{96 + 27 + 27 + 9 + 9}{8} = \frac{168}{8} = 21.$$

The difference tells us something too. Each $D_4$-orbit is either a single rotation orbit (colourings equal to a rotation of their mirror image) or the union of two rotation orbits (a mirror-image pair). If $c$ orbits split, then $24 = 21 + c$, so exactly $3$ colourings are "chiral" pairs that only a reflection can match up.

blocks.body:
- The converse of Lagrange is false. The group $A_4$ of even permutations of four objects (equivalently, the rotations of a regular tetrahedron) has order $12$ but no subgroup of order $6$.
- Composition conventions differ between books: some write $rs$ for "first $r$, then $s$". Since groups need not be abelian, check the convention before multiplying.
- In Burnside's lemma the average is over group elements, not over types of elements. Each type must be weighted by how many elements it contains (in the cube, $8$ rotations of the $120^\circ$ type, not $1$).
- A subset whose size divides $|G|$ need not be a subgroup; closure and inverses must be checked. Likewise, a set with an operation is not a group until closure is verified, as the example of multiplication modulo $6$ shows.
- Orbit–stabiliser needs a genuine action: the symmetries must map the set $X$ into itself and satisfy $g\cdot(h\cdot x) = (gh)\cdot x$.

Lagrange's theorem is the abstract reason behind [[fermat-euler]], and the finer fact that $(\mathbb Z/p)^\times$ is always cyclic is the subject of [[order-primroot]]. The next step in the theory is [[group-homomorphisms]]: maps that preserve the operation, normal subgroups, and quotient groups such as $\mathbb Z/n = \mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$. Actions are developed further in [[group-actions]] (the class equation and the Sylow theorems grow out of orbit–stabiliser).

Adding a second operation leads to [[rings]] and fields ([[finite-fields]], [[fields-ext]]), and [[galois]] theory attaches a group of symmetries to the roots of a polynomial. In physics, continuous groups of symmetries such as the rotation group and the unitary groups $SU(N)$ are the gauge groups of [[yang-mills]] theory.

1. Show that every group of even order contains an element of order $2$.
2. List all subgroups of $\mathbb Z/12$ and check that their orders divide $12$.
3. Prove that a group of prime order $p$ is cyclic, and that every element other than $e$ generates it.
4. Use Burnside's lemma to count necklaces of $6$ beads in $2$ colours, where two necklaces are the same if one is a rotation of the other.

blocks.body:
A farmer has $40$ metres of fence and wants a rectangular pen of the largest possible area. Sides $10 \times 10$ give $100$ square metres, $12 \times 8$ gives $96$, $15 \times 5$ gives $75$. The square wins, and the reason is a single inequality: for a fixed sum, a product of non-negative numbers is largest when the numbers are equal.

That inequality, the arithmetic mean–geometric mean (AM–GM) inequality, is the most used tool in elementary inequalities. This page proves it for any number of terms, shows how to apply it (the art is in choosing what to apply it to), and places it inside a whole ladder of means, the power means.

blocks.title: Two numbers
blocks.body:
For $x, y \ge 0$, the square $(\sqrt x - \sqrt y)^2$ is non-negative. Expanding,

$$x + y - 2\sqrt{xy} \ge 0, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \frac{x+y}{2} \ge \sqrt{xy},$$

with equality exactly when $\sqrt x = \sqrt y$, i.e. $x = y$.

There is also a picture. Draw a circle with diameter $AB$ and pick $P$ on $AB$ with $AP = x$, $PB = y$. The perpendicular to $AB$ at $P$ meets the circle at $Q$. Triangle $AQB$ has a right angle at $Q$, and the altitude from the right angle satisfies $PQ^2 = AP \cdot PB = xy$. A half-chord is never longer than the radius, so $\sqrt{xy} = PQ \le \tfrac{x+y}{2}$, with equality when $P$ is the centre.

For the farmer: if the sides are $a$ and $b$ with $a + b = 20$, the area is $ab \le \big(\tfrac{a+b}{2}\big)^2 = 100$, with equality only for $a = b = 10$.

blocks.title: AM–GM inequality
blocks.body:
For real numbers $x_1, \dots, x_n \ge 0$,

$$\frac{x_1+\cdots+x_n}{n} \ge \sqrt[n]{x_1\cdots x_n},$$

with equality if and only if $x_1 = x_2 = \cdots = x_n$.

Let $A = (x_1 + \cdots + x_n)/n$.

If some $x_i = 0$, the right side is $0 \le A$, and equality would force $A = 0$, i.e. all $x_i = 0$. So assume from now on that all $x_i > 0$.

If all the $x_i$ equal $A$, both sides equal $A$. Otherwise, since $A$ is their average, some $x_i$ is below $A$ and some $x_j$ is above it. Replace the pair $(x_i, x_j)$ by $(A,\ x_i + x_j - A)$. Three things happen:

1. The sum, hence the mean $A$, is unchanged.
2. The new numbers are positive, since $x_i + x_j - A > x_i > 0$.
3. The product of the pair goes up, because
$$A(x_i + x_j - A) - x_ix_j = (A - x_i)(x_j - A) > 0.$$
The other numbers are positive and untouched, so the whole product strictly increases.

Each such step makes at least one more entry equal to $A$. When $n - 1$ entries equal $A$ the last one does too (the sum is $nA$), so after at most $n-1$ steps every entry is $A$ and the product is $A^n$. The product only increased along the way, so the original product was less than $A^n$. Taking $n$-th roots: if the $x_i$ are not all equal, the geometric mean is strictly less than $A$.
blocks.title: Proof by smoothing
Weighted AM–GM
blocks.body:
Often the terms deserve different weights. If $w_1, \dots, w_n \ge 0$ with $w_1 + \cdots + w_n = 1$ and $x_i \ge 0$, then

$$w_1x_1 + \cdots + w_nx_n \ge x_1^{w_1}x_2^{w_2}\cdots x_n^{w_n}.$$

For rational weights this is ordinary AM–GM in disguise. Write $w_i = m_i/N$ with whole numbers $m_i$ and apply AM–GM to $N$ numbers consisting of $m_i$ copies of $x_i$. For instance, with two copies of $a$ and one of $b$,

$$\frac{2a + b}{3} = \frac{a + a + b}{3} \ge \sqrt[3]{a^2 b}.$$

Irrational weights follow by approximating with rational ones, or directly from the concavity of the logarithm (see [[convexity]]). As before, equality holds exactly when all $x_i$ with positive weight are equal.

blocks.title: How to use it: make the product constant
blocks.body:
AM–GM turns a sum into a product. It is useful when the product is something you control, typically a constant.

Minimise $x + \tfrac4x$ for $x > 0$. The two terms have product $4$, so $x + \tfrac4x \ge 2\sqrt{4} = 4$, with equality when $x = \tfrac4x$, i.e. $x = 2$. Since equality is attained, the minimum is $4$.

The equality case is also a guide. Before splitting terms, guess where the extremum is, then split so that all the pieces are equal there. The next example shows a case where the naive split fails.

blocks.title: Power means
blocks.body:
For positive reals $x_1, \dots, x_n$ and a real number $p \ne 0$, the power mean of order $p$ is

$$M_p(x) = \Big(\tfrac1n\textstyle\sum x_i^p\Big)^{1/p},$$

and $M_0(x)$ is defined to be the geometric mean $\sqrt[n]{x_1\cdots x_n}$. Special cases: $M_1$ is the arithmetic mean, $M_2$ the quadratic mean (root mean square), and $M_{-1} = n/(\tfrac1{x_1} + \cdots + \tfrac1{x_n})$ the harmonic mean. As $p \to +\infty$, $M_p \to \max x_i$, and as $p \to -\infty$, $M_p \to \min x_i$.

Taking the geometric mean as $M_0$ is not arbitrary: $M_p(x) \to \sqrt[n]{x_1\cdots x_n}$ as $p \to 0$, so it fills the gap continuously.

blocks.title: Power mean inequality
blocks.body:
For positive reals $x_1, \dots, x_n$, the power mean $M_p(x)$ is increasing in $p$: if $p < q$ then $M_p(x) \le M_q(x)$, with equality only when all $x_i$ are equal. In particular

$$\min x_i \le \frac{n}{\sum 1/x_i} \le \sqrt[n]{x_1\cdots x_n} \le \frac{\sum x_i}{n} \le \sqrt{\frac{\sum x_i^2}{n}} \le \max x_i.$$

The middle inequality GM $\le$ AM is AM–GM.

AM $\le$ QM: with $A = \tfrac1n\sum x_i$,
$$0 \le \frac1n\sum (x_i - A)^2 = \frac1n\sum x_i^2 - 2A\cdot A + A^2 = \frac1n\sum x_i^2 - A^2.$$

HM $\le$ GM: apply AM–GM to the numbers $1/x_i$: $\tfrac1n\sum \tfrac1{x_i} \ge \big(\prod \tfrac1{x_i}\big)^{1/n}$, and take reciprocals of both sides.

The two outer inequalities hold because every mean of the numbers lies between the smallest and the largest. Equality in each step forces all $x_i$ to be equal.

The general statement for arbitrary $p < q$ is a consequence of Jensen's inequality and is proved on the [[convexity]] page; we do not repeat it here.
blocks.title: Proof of the chain

blocks.body:
Prove that for all $a, b, c \ge 0$,
$$(a+b)(b+c)(c+a) \ge 8abc.$$
When does equality hold?
blocks.solution:
By AM–GM for two numbers, $a + b \ge 2\sqrt{ab}$, $b + c \ge 2\sqrt{bc}$, $c + a \ge 2\sqrt{ca}$. All six sides are non-negative, so we may multiply:

$$(a+b)(b+c)(c+a) \ge 8\sqrt{ab\cdot bc\cdot ca} = 8abc.$$

If $a, b, c > 0$, equality needs equality in each factor, so $a = b = c$. If some variable is $0$ the right side is $0$, and the left side is $0$ only when two of the variables vanish. So equality holds exactly when $a = b = c$ or at least two of $a, b, c$ are zero.

blocks.body: Find the minimum of $f(x) = x^2 + \dfrac{16}{x}$ for $x > 0$.
blocks.solution:
The naive two-term AM–GM gives $x^2 + \tfrac{16}{x} \ge 2\sqrt{16x} = 8\sqrt x$, which depends on $x$ and so proves nothing about the minimum.

The product must be constant. Since $x^2$ has degree $2$ and $\tfrac1x$ degree $-1$, split the second term in two:

$$x^2 + \frac8x + \frac8x \ge 3\sqrt[3]{x^2\cdot\frac8x\cdot\frac8x} = 3\sqrt[3]{64} = 12.$$

Equality requires $x^2 = 8/x$, i.e. $x^3 = 8$, $x = 2$, and indeed $f(2) = 4 + 8 = 12$. So the minimum is $12$, attained at $x = 2$. (Calculus agrees: $f'(x) = 2x - 16/x^2$ vanishes at $x = 2$.)
blocks.title: Splitting terms with the equality case in mind

blocks.body:
Prove that for $a, b, c \ge 0$,
$$a^3 + b^3 + c^3 \ge a^2b + b^2c + c^2a.$$
blocks.solution:
Each term on the right is a weighted geometric mean of cubes: $a^2b = (a^3)^{2/3}(b^3)^{1/3}$. Weighted AM–GM with weights $\tfrac23, \tfrac13$ gives

$$\frac{2a^3 + b^3}{3} \ge a^2b,\qquad \frac{2b^3 + c^3}{3} \ge b^2c,\qquad \frac{2c^3 + a^3}{3} \ge c^2a.$$

Adding the three, the left sides total $\tfrac{3(a^3+b^3+c^3)}{3} = a^3 + b^3 + c^3$. Equality needs $a = b = c$.

The pattern generalises: to bound a monomial such as $a^2b$ by a sum of pure powers, read off the weights from its exponents.
blocks.title: Weighted AM–GM

blocks.body:
Positive reals $a, b, c$ satisfy $abc = 1$. Prove that
$$a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \ge a + b + c.$$
blocks.solution:
Let $s = a + b + c$. Two rungs of the ladder are needed.

QM $\ge$ AM, squared and multiplied by $3$: $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \ge \tfrac{s^2}{3}$.

AM $\ge$ GM: $\tfrac s3 \ge \sqrt[3]{abc} = 1$.

Combining, $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \ge \tfrac{s^2}{3} = s\cdot\tfrac s3 \ge s$, which is the claim. Equality throughout forces $a = b = c$, and with $abc = 1$ that means $a = b = c = 1$.

Notice the role of the constraint: the inequality is not homogeneous (the two sides have different degrees), and $abc = 1$ is what lets AM–GM bridge the degree gap.
blocks.title: Climbing the ladder of means

blocks.body:
- Non-negativity matters. $x + \tfrac1x \ge 2$ is false for $x = -1$, and $\sqrt[n]{x_1\cdots x_n}$ need not even make sense for negative numbers.
- A bound is only a minimum if the equality case is allowed. For $x \ge 2$, AM–GM still says $x + \tfrac1x \ge 2$, but equality needs $x = 1$, which is excluded; the true minimum on $[2, \infty)$ is $\tfrac52$, at $x = 2$.
- If the product of the terms is not constant (as in the naive attempt on $x^2 + 16/x$), AM–GM gives a bound that depends on the variable, which usually proves nothing.
- Power means of order $p \le 0$ require all $x_i > 0$; for $p > 0$ zeros are allowed.

The inequality AM $\le$ QM is the simplest case of [[cauchy-schwarz]], and the general power mean inequality and weighted AM–GM are both instances of Jensen's inequality for convex functions ([[convexity]]). Muirhead's inequality, met in [[symmetric-ineq]], is a far-reaching generalisation of AM–GM for symmetric sums.

In geometry AM–GM gives the isoperimetric property of the equilateral triangle ([[geo-inequalities]]). By Heron's formula a triangle with sides $a, b, c$ and semiperimeter $s$ has area $\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$. The three numbers $s-a$, $s-b$, $s-c$ are positive with sum $s$, so their product is at most $(s/3)^3$, giving

$$\text{Area} \le \frac{s^2}{3\sqrt3},$$

with equality only for the equilateral triangle: among triangles of a given perimeter, the equilateral one encloses the most area.

blocks.body:
In the plane, the dot product of two vectors is $u\cdot v = |u|\,|v|\cos\theta$, and since $|\cos\theta| \le 1$ it never exceeds the product of the lengths. Written in coordinates, $(u_1v_1 + u_2v_2)^2 \le (u_1^2 + u_2^2)(v_1^2 + v_2^2)$. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality says the same holds for lists of any length, where there is no picture to lean on.

This page proves Cauchy–Schwarz, derives its most useful competition form (the Engel form, sometimes called Titu's lemma), generalises it to Hölder's inequality, and adds the rearrangement inequality, which compares sums of products when the order of the terms is shuffled.

blocks.title: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
blocks.body:
For real numbers $a_1, \dots, a_n$ and $b_1, \dots, b_n$,

$$\Big(\sum a_ib_i\Big)^2 \le \sum a_i^2 \sum b_i^2.$$

Equality holds if and only if the lists are proportional: one of $(a_i)$, $(b_i)$ is a scalar multiple of the other (this includes the case where one list is all zeros).

Put $A = \sum a_i^2$, $B = \sum b_i^2$, $C = \sum a_ib_i$. If $A = 0$ every $a_i$ is $0$ and both sides vanish. Otherwise consider, for real $t$,

$$f(t) = \sum (a_it - b_i)^2 = At^2 - 2Ct + B.$$

As a sum of squares, $f(t) \ge 0$ for every $t$. A quadratic with positive leading coefficient that never goes negative has at most one real root, so its discriminant is not positive: $4C^2 - 4AB \le 0$, which is $C^2 \le AB$.

Equality $C^2 = AB$ means the discriminant is zero, so $f$ has a real root $t_0$. Then every square $(a_it_0 - b_i)^2$ is zero, i.e. $b_i = t_0a_i$ for all $i$. Conversely, proportional lists clearly give equality.
blocks.title: Proof by a quadratic that cannot go negative
An identity behind the inequality
blocks.body:
There is an exact formula for the gap, called Lagrange's identity:

$$\sum a_i^2\sum b_i^2 - \Big(\sum a_ib_i\Big)^2 = \sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(a_ib_j - a_jb_i)^2.$$

To see it, expand the left side: the products $a_i^2b_i^2$ cancel, and what remains is $\sum_{i\ne j}a_i^2b_j^2 - \sum_{i \ne j}a_ib_ia_jb_j$, which regroups pair by pair into the squares on the right. This gives a second proof of Cauchy–Schwarz and makes the equality case transparent: all the $2\times2$ determinants $a_ib_j - a_jb_i$ must vanish. For $n = 2$ the right side is $(a_1b_2 - a_2b_1)^2$, the squared area of the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors, matching $|u|^2|v|^2\sin^2\theta$.

blocks.title: Engel form
blocks.body:
For real numbers $a_1, \dots, a_n$ and positive reals $b_1, \dots, b_n$,

$$\sum \frac{a_i^2}{b_i} \ge \frac{(\sum a_i)^2}{\sum b_i},$$

with equality if and only if $a_1/b_1 = a_2/b_2 = \cdots = a_n/b_n$.

Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the lists $a_i/\sqrt{b_i}$ and $\sqrt{b_i}$ (this is where $b_i > 0$ is used):

$$\Big(\sum a_i\Big)^2 = \Big(\sum \frac{a_i}{\sqrt{b_i}}\cdot\sqrt{b_i}\Big)^2 \le \sum\frac{a_i^2}{b_i}\cdot\sum b_i.$$

Divide by $\sum b_i > 0$. Equality requires $a_i/\sqrt{b_i} = t\sqrt{b_i}$ for a common $t$, i.e. $a_i/b_i = t$ for all $i$.

blocks.title: When to reach for the Engel form
blocks.body:
The Engel form is built for sums of fractions. Its typical use: a sum $\sum x_i/y_i$ can be rewritten as $\sum x_i^2/(x_iy_i)$ (when $x_i > 0$), so that the numerators are squares and the inequality collapses the whole sum into one fraction. The art is in choosing the numerators so that $\sum a_i$ is something you know, and the equality condition (all ratios $a_i/b_i$ equal) tells you whether the bound can be sharp.

A quick illustration: for positive $x, y$, $\tfrac1x + \tfrac1y = \tfrac{1^2}{x} + \tfrac{1^2}{y} \ge \tfrac{(1+1)^2}{x+y} = \tfrac{4}{x+y}$.

blocks.title: Hölder's inequality
blocks.body:
Let $p, q > 1$ with $\tfrac1p + \tfrac1q = 1$, and let $a_i, b_i \ge 0$. Then

$$\sum a_ib_i \le \Big(\sum a_i^p\Big)^{1/p}\Big(\sum b_i^q\Big)^{1/q}.$$

The case $p = q = 2$ is Cauchy–Schwarz. A three-list version often used in competitions: for $x_i, y_i, z_i \ge 0$,

$$\Big(\sum x_i^3\Big)\Big(\sum y_i^3\Big)\Big(\sum z_i^3\Big) \ge \Big(\sum x_iy_iz_i\Big)^3.$$

First Young's inequality: for $x, y \ge 0$, weighted [[amgm|AM–GM]] applied to $x^p$ and $y^q$ with weights $\tfrac1p$ and $\tfrac1q$ gives

$$\frac{x^p}{p} + \frac{y^q}{q} \ge (x^p)^{1/p}(y^q)^{1/q} = xy.$$

Now let $X = (\sum a_i^p)^{1/p}$ and $Y = (\sum b_i^q)^{1/q}$. If $X = 0$ or $Y = 0$ one list is all zeros and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise apply Young to $x = a_i/X$ and $y = b_i/Y$ and add over $i$:

$$\frac{\sum a_ib_i}{XY} \le \frac1p\cdot\frac{\sum a_i^p}{X^p} + \frac1q\cdot\frac{\sum b_i^q}{Y^q} = \frac1p + \frac1q = 1.$$

The three-list version is proved the same way, using $xyz \le \tfrac13(x^3 + y^3 + z^3)$ (AM–GM) after dividing each list by the cube root of its sum of cubes.
blocks.title: Proof via weighted AM–GM
Rearrangement: ordering is everything
blocks.body: Suppose you are paid $a_i$ euros per item for items of $n$ kinds, and you may decide which kind gets which quantity from a fixed list $b_1, \dots, b_n$. Common sense says: put the largest quantity on the best-paid item, the next largest on the next, and so on. The rearrangement inequality confirms it, and also says the opposite pairing is the worst.

blocks.title: Rearrangement inequality
blocks.body:
Let $a_1 \le a_2 \le \cdots \le a_n$ and $b_1 \le b_2 \le \cdots \le b_n$ be real numbers, and let $\sigma$ be any permutation of $\{1, \dots, n\}$. Then

$$a_1b_n + a_2b_{n-1} + \cdots + a_nb_1 \;\le\; \sum_{i=1}^n a_ib_{\sigma(i)} \;\le\; a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + \cdots + a_nb_n.$$

So similarly ordered pairing gives the largest sum and oppositely ordered pairing the smallest.

Write $c_i = b_{\sigma(i)}$, an arrangement of the $b$'s. If the list $c$ is not in increasing order, there is a position $i$ with $c_i > c_{i+1}$. Swap these two entries. The sum changes by

$$\big(a_ic_{i+1} + a_{i+1}c_i\big) - \big(a_ic_i + a_{i+1}c_{i+1}\big) = (a_{i+1} - a_i)(c_i - c_{i+1}) \ge 0,$$

so it does not decrease. Each swap reduces by one the number of pairs $j < k$ with $c_j > c_k$, so after finitely many swaps $c$ is in increasing order, i.e. $c = (b_1, \dots, b_n)$, and the sum has become $\sum a_ib_i$. This proves the upper bound.

For the lower bound apply the upper bound to $a$ and the increasing list $-b_n \le -b_{n-1} \le \cdots \le -b_1$, then multiply by $-1$.

Positive reals $x, y, z$ satisfy $x + y + z = 1$. Find the minimum of
$$\frac1x + \frac4y + \frac9z.$$
blocks.solution:
Write the numerators as squares, $1 = 1^2$, $4 = 2^2$, $9 = 3^2$, and apply the Engel form:

$$\frac{1^2}{x} + \frac{2^2}{y} + \frac{3^2}{z} \ge \frac{(1+2+3)^2}{x+y+z} = 36.$$

Equality requires $\tfrac1x = \tfrac2y = \tfrac3z$, i.e. $x : y : z = 1 : 2 : 3$, and with the constraint $x = \tfrac16$, $y = \tfrac13$, $z = \tfrac12$. Then the expression is $6 + 12 + 18 = 36$, so the minimum is $36$.
blocks.title: Engel form with a linear constraint

blocks.body:
Prove that for positive reals $a, b, c$,
$$\frac{a}{b+c} + \frac{b}{c+a} + \frac{c}{a+b} \ge \frac32.$$
blocks.solution:
Make the numerators squares by multiplying top and bottom by $a$, $b$, $c$, then use the Engel form:

$$\sum\frac{a^2}{a(b+c)} \ge \frac{(a+b+c)^2}{a(b+c) + b(c+a) + c(a+b)} = \frac{(a+b+c)^2}{2(ab+bc+ca)}.$$

It remains to show $(a+b+c)^2 \ge 3(ab+bc+ca)$. Expanding, this is $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \ge ab + bc + ca$, which is $\tfrac12\big((a-b)^2 + (b-c)^2 + (c-a)^2\big) \ge 0$. Hence the sum is at least $\tfrac{3(ab+bc+ca)}{2(ab+bc+ca)} = \tfrac32$, with equality when $a = b = c$.
blocks.title: Nesbitt's inequality

blocks.body:
(a) Let $a_1 \le \cdots \le a_n$ and $b_1 \le \cdots \le b_n$. Prove
$$n\sum a_ib_i \ge \Big(\sum a_i\Big)\Big(\sum b_i\Big).$$
(b) Deduce that $(a+b+c)(a^2+b^2+c^2) \le 3(a^3+b^3+c^3)$ for $a, b, c \ge 0$.
blocks.solution:
(a) For each shift $k = 0, 1, \dots, n-1$, the pairing $a_i \leftrightarrow b_{i+k}$ (indices taken cyclically, so $b_{n+1} = b_1$ and so on) is one arrangement of the $b$'s. By rearrangement each is at most the sorted pairing:

$$\sum_{i=1}^n a_ib_{i+k} \le \sum_{i=1}^n a_ib_i \qquad (k = 0, \dots, n-1).$$

Add these $n$ inequalities. On the left every product $a_ib_j$ appears exactly once, so the left side totals $(\sum a_i)(\sum b_j)$; the right side totals $n\sum a_ib_i$.

(b) For non-negative numbers, the lists $a, b, c$ and $a^2, b^2, c^2$ are ordered the same way (squaring preserves order on $[0,\infty)$). Sort both and apply (a) with $n = 3$: $3(a\cdot a^2 + b\cdot b^2 + c\cdot c^2) \ge (a+b+c)(a^2+b^2+c^2)$.
blocks.title: Chebyshev's sum inequality from rearrangement

blocks.body:
Positive reals $a, b, c$ satisfy $a + b + c = 3$. Prove that
$$\frac1{a^2} + \frac1{b^2} + \frac1{c^2} \ge 3.$$
blocks.solution:
Apply the three-list Hölder inequality to the lists with cubes $x_i^3 = 1/a_i^2$, $y_i^3 = a_i$, $z_i^3 = a_i$. Then $x_iy_iz_i = (a_i^{-2}\cdot a_i\cdot a_i)^{1/3} = 1$, so

$$\Big(\sum\frac1{a^2}\Big)\Big(\sum a\Big)\Big(\sum a\Big) \ge (1 + 1 + 1)^3 = 27.$$

With $\sum a = 3$ this reads $9\sum \tfrac1{a^2} \ge 27$, which is the claim. Equality needs the three lists to be proportional, which happens at $a = b = c = 1$.

The pattern to remember: Hölder lets you multiply the target sum by suitable sums you already know, chosen so that the product of the terms is constant.
blocks.title: Hölder with three lists

blocks.body:
- The Engel form needs every $b_i > 0$. With $a = (1, 1)$ and $b = (1, -\tfrac12)$ the left side is $1 - 2 = -1$ while the right side is $\tfrac{4}{1/2} = 8$.
- Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz means the lists are proportional, not equal. In the first example the equality point is $x : y : z = 1 : 2 : 3$, not $x = y = z$.
- Hölder's exponents must be conjugate, $\tfrac1p + \tfrac1q = 1$, and the terms non-negative.
- Rearrangement compares arrangements of the same two lists. It needs both lists sorted in the same direction for the upper bound; for numbers of mixed sign, transformations such as squaring may change the order.

Cauchy–Schwarz is the defining inequality of [[inner-products]]: in any inner-product space $|\langle u, v\rangle| \le \|u\|\,\|v\|$, which is what makes "angle" meaningful in high dimensions. Its integral form $\big(\int fg\big)^2 \le \int f^2\int g^2$ was published by Bunyakovsky (1859) and by Schwarz (1888); Cauchy had stated the finite-sum version in his Cours d'analyse of 1821. In probability it says that a correlation coefficient lies in $[-1, 1]$ ([[random-variables]]). In analytic number theory it is everywhere, for instance in the [[large-sieve]] and in bounds for [[exponential-sums]].

Among olympiad tools it sits next to [[amgm]] (the special case AM $\le$ QM is the Engel form with all $b_i = 1$) and [[convexity]], and it is a standard step in [[symmetric-ineq|symmetric inequalities]] and [[geo-inequalities|geometric inequalities]].

blocks.body:
Average two numbers and then square, or square and then average: which is bigger? For $1$ and $5$, $\big(\tfrac{1+5}{2}\big)^2 = 9$ while $\tfrac{1^2 + 5^2}{2} = 13$. Squaring first always wins, and the reason is geometric: the graph of $y = x^2$ bends upwards, so the chord joining two points of the graph lies above the graph.

Functions whose graphs bend this way are called convex, and this one property explains a remarkable number of inequalities: AM–GM, the power mean inequality, many trigonometric bounds in triangles. This page develops Jensen's inequality, the tangent line trick for functions that are convex only in part of their range, and Karamata's majorization inequality, which compares two whole lists of numbers rather than a list and its average.

blocks.title: Convex function
blocks.body:
A function $f$ defined on an interval $I$ is convex if for all $x, y \in I$ and all $t \in [0,1]$

$$f\big(tx + (1-t)y\big) \le tf(x) + (1-t)f(y).$$

It is strictly convex if the inequality is strict whenever $x \ne y$ and $0 < t < 1$, and concave if $-f$ is convex.

Meaning: as $t$ runs from $0$ to $1$, the point $tx + (1-t)y$ runs between $y$ and $x$, and the right side is the height of the chord above it; the graph never rises above any of its chords.

blocks.title: Recognising convexity: the second derivative
blocks.body:
Checking the definition directly is tedious, and for smooth functions there is a better test. Intuitively, convex means "the slope keeps increasing", i.e. $f'$ is non-decreasing, i.e. $f'' \ge 0$.

Useful convex functions: $x^2$ and $e^x$ on $\mathbb R$; $x^p$ for $p \ge 1$ on $[0, \infty)$; $1/x$, $-\ln x$ and $x\ln x$ on $(0, \infty)$. Concave ones: $\ln x$ and $\sqrt x$ on $(0, \infty)$, and $\sin x$ on $[0, \pi]$, since $\sin'' = -\sin \le 0$ there.

blocks.title: Second derivative test
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be twice differentiable on an open interval $I$. If $f''(x) \ge 0$ for all $x \in I$, then $f$ is convex on $I$; if $f''(x) > 0$ for all $x \in I$, then $f$ is strictly convex. Moreover, in either case $f$ lies above each of its tangent lines:

$$f(x) \ge f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)\qquad\text{for all } a, x \in I,$$

strictly for $x \ne a$ when $f'' > 0$.

Since $f'' \ge 0$, the [[mvt|mean value theorem]] applied to $f'$ shows that $f'$ is non-decreasing (strictly increasing if $f'' > 0$).

Chords. Take $x < y$ in $I$ and $0 < t < 1$, and put $z = tx + (1-t)y$, so $x < z < y$, with $z - x = (1-t)(y - x)$ and $y - z = t(y - x)$. By the mean value theorem there are $\xi \in (x, z)$ and $\eta \in (z, y)$ with

$$f'(\xi) = \frac{f(z) - f(x)}{(1-t)(y-x)},\qquad f'(\eta) = \frac{f(y) - f(z)}{t(y-x)}.$$

As $\xi < \eta$, we have $f'(\xi) \le f'(\eta)$. Clearing the positive denominators gives $t\big(f(z) - f(x)\big) \le (1-t)\big(f(y) - f(z)\big)$, which rearranges to $f(z) \le tf(x) + (1-t)f(y)$. If $f'' > 0$ the inequality $f'(\xi) < f'(\eta)$ is strict, and so is the conclusion.

Tangents. Let $g(x) = f(x) - f(a) - f'(a)(x - a)$. Then $g(a) = 0$ and $g'(x) = f'(x) - f'(a)$, which is $\le 0$ for $x < a$ and $\ge 0$ for $x > a$. So $g$ decreases up to $a$ and increases after it, and its minimum value is $g(a) = 0$. When $f'$ is strictly increasing, $g$ is strictly monotone on each side and $g(x) > 0$ for $x \ne a$.

blocks.title: Jensen's inequality
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be convex on an interval $I$, let $x_1, \dots, x_n \in I$, and let $w_1, \dots, w_n \ge 0$ with $\sum w_i = 1$. Then

$$f\Big(\sum w_ix_i\Big) \le \sum w_i f(x_i)\qquad (f \text{ convex},\ \textstyle\sum w_i = 1).$$

If $f$ is strictly convex and all $w_i > 0$, equality holds only when $x_1 = \cdots = x_n$. For concave $f$ the inequality reverses. With equal weights $w_i = \tfrac1n$: $f(\text{mean}) \le \text{mean of } f$.

Weights equal to $0$ can be dropped, so assume all $w_i > 0$. For $n = 1$ there is nothing to prove, and $n = 2$ is the definition. Suppose the statement holds for $n - 1$ points, and let $n \ge 3$. Put $W = 1 - w_n = w_1 + \cdots + w_{n-1} > 0$ and

$$y = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{w_i}{W}x_i,$$

a weighted average of points of $I$, hence itself in $I$. Then $\sum_{i=1}^n w_ix_i = Wy + w_nx_n$, and

$$f\Big(\sum w_ix_i\Big) \le Wf(y) + w_nf(x_n) \le W\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{w_i}{W}f(x_i) + w_nf(x_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n w_if(x_i),$$

using the definition of convexity (two points, weights $W$ and $w_n$) and then the induction hypothesis (the weights $w_i/W$ sum to $1$).

Equality case: if $f$ is strictly convex, equality in the whole chain forces equality in both steps (the second step is multiplied by $W > 0$). By induction the second gives $x_1 = \cdots = x_{n-1}$, so $y$ equals this common value, and the first gives $x_n = y$.
blocks.title: Proof by induction
AM–GM and power means as Jensen
blocks.body:
The logarithm is concave on $(0, \infty)$, since $(\ln x)'' = -1/x^2 < 0$. Jensen for concave functions gives, for positive $x_i$ and weights $w_i$ summing to $1$,

$$\ln\Big(\sum w_ix_i\Big) \ge \sum w_i\ln x_i = \ln\Big(\prod x_i^{w_i}\Big),$$

and exponentiating yields weighted [[amgm|AM–GM]]: $\sum w_ix_i \ge \prod x_i^{w_i}$, with equality only when all $x_i$ are equal (strict concavity).

The power mean inequality follows similarly. For $0 < p < q$ the function $\varphi(t) = t^{q/p}$ is convex on $(0, \infty)$ since $q/p > 1$. Applying Jensen with equal weights to the numbers $y_i = x_i^p$:

$$\Big(\frac1n\sum x_i^p\Big)^{q/p} \le \frac1n\sum x_i^q,$$

and taking $q$-th roots gives $M_p \le M_q$. Other sign patterns of $p, q$ are handled the same way with the appropriate convex or concave power.

blocks.title: The tangent line trick
blocks.body:
Often the function in a problem is not convex on the whole range, so Jensen does not apply, yet the answer is still "all variables equal". If the variables have a fixed sum and the expected equality point is $x = m$, compare $f$ with its tangent line at $m$:

$$f(x) \ge f(m) + f'(m)(x - m)\quad\text{for every allowed } x.$$

If this one-variable inequality can be checked (usually by factoring, with a square $(x - m)^2$ appearing), summing it over the variables kills the linear terms because the sum is fixed. Example 2 below shows the method.

blocks.title: Majorization
blocks.body:
Let $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ and $y = (y_1, \dots, y_n)$ be lists sorted in decreasing order: $x_1 \ge \cdots \ge x_n$ and $y_1 \ge \cdots \ge y_n$. We say $x$ majorizes $y$, written $x \succ y$, if

$$x_1 + \cdots + x_k \ge y_1 + \cdots + y_k\quad (k = 1, \dots, n-1)\qquad\text{and}\qquad x_1 + \cdots + x_n = y_1 + \cdots + y_n.$$

Meaning: $y$ is a more evenly spread version of $x$ with the same total. For example $(3,0,0) \succ (2,1,0) \succ (1,1,1)$, and any list with sum $ns$ majorizes the constant list $(s, \dots, s)$, because the $k$ largest entries of a list have average at least the overall average.

blocks.title: Three-chord lemma
blocks.body:
For $u \ne v$ write $s(u,v) = \dfrac{f(u) - f(v)}{u - v}$ for the slope of the chord. If $f$ is convex on $I$ and $u < v < w$ are in $I$, then

$$s(u,v) \le s(u,w) \le s(v,w).$$

Consequently $s(u,v)$, which is symmetric in $u$ and $v$, is non-decreasing in each variable.

Write $v = tu + (1-t)w$ with $t = \tfrac{w - v}{w - u} \in (0,1)$; then $v - u = (1-t)(w - u)$ and $w - v = t(w - u)$. Convexity gives $f(v) \le tf(u) + (1-t)f(w)$.

Subtracting $f(u)$: $f(v) - f(u) \le (1-t)\big(f(w) - f(u)\big)$; dividing by $v - u = (1-t)(w-u)$ gives $s(u,v) \le s(u,w)$.

Subtracting $f(w)$: $f(v) - f(w) \le t\big(f(u) - f(w)\big)$, i.e. $f(w) - f(v) \ge t\big(f(w) - f(u)\big)$; dividing by $w - v = t(w - u)$ gives $s(v,w) \ge s(u,w)$.

For the monotonicity, fix one argument $v$ and compare two values $u < u'$ of the other: whichever of the three orders $u < u' < v$, $u < v < u'$, $v < u < u'$ occurs, the lemma applied to the three points gives $s(u, v) \le s(u', v)$.

blocks.title: Karamata's inequality
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be convex on an interval $I$, and let $x, y \in I^n$ be sorted in decreasing order with $x \succ y$. Then

$$f(x_1) + \cdots + f(x_n) \ge f(y_1) + \cdots + f(y_n).$$

We assume $f$ is differentiable; the general case is the same argument with one-sided derivatives. Define $c_i = s(x_i, y_i)$ if $x_i \ne y_i$ and $c_i = f'(x_i)$ if $x_i = y_i$. In both cases $f(x_i) - f(y_i) = c_i(x_i - y_i)$.

The extended slope function (with $f'(u)$ as the value at $u = v$) is still non-decreasing in each variable, because $f'(u)$ is a limit of chord slopes $s(u, v)$ and inequalities survive limits. Since $x_i \ge x_{i+1}$ and $y_i \ge y_{i+1}$, it follows that $c_1 \ge c_2 \ge \cdots \ge c_n$.

Let $X_k = x_1 + \cdots + x_k$ and $Y_k = y_1 + \cdots + y_k$, with $X_0 = Y_0 = 0$, and $D_k = X_k - Y_k$. Majorization says $D_k \ge 0$ for $k < n$ and $D_n = 0$. Then $x_i - y_i = D_i - D_{i-1}$ and

$$\sum_{i=1}^n \big(f(x_i) - f(y_i)\big) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i(D_i - D_{i-1}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(c_i - c_{i+1})D_i + c_nD_n.$$

Every term $(c_i - c_{i+1})D_i$ is a product of two non-negative numbers and $D_n = 0$, so the sum is $\ge 0$.
blocks.title: Proof (for differentiable f) by summation by parts
Smoothing
blocks.body: Karamata explains a common olympiad move. If you replace two variables $x_i > x_j$ by two values closer together with the same sum, the new list is majorized by the old one, so for convex $f$ the sum $\sum f(x_i)$ does not go up. Repeating such moves pushes the list towards all-equal, which is why "the minimum of a sum of convex terms with fixed total is at the equal point" and "the maximum is at the extreme spread". The proof of [[amgm|AM–GM]] by smoothing is an instance of the same idea.

Prove that in every triangle with angles $A, B, C$,
$$\sin A + \sin B + \sin C \le \frac{3\sqrt3}{2}.$$
blocks.solution:
The angles lie in $(0, \pi)$ and sum to $\pi$. On $(0, \pi)$, $\sin'' = -\sin < 0$, so $\sin$ is strictly concave there. Jensen with equal weights (reversed for concave functions) gives

$$\frac{\sin A + \sin B + \sin C}{3} \le \sin\Big(\frac{A + B + C}{3}\Big) = \sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}.$$

Multiply by $3$. By strict concavity equality holds only for $A = B = C$, the equilateral triangle.
blocks.title: Jensen in a triangle

blocks.body:
Positive reals $a, b, c$ satisfy $a + b + c = 3$. Prove that
$$\frac1{1+a^2} + \frac1{1+b^2} + \frac1{1+c^2} \ge \frac32.$$
blocks.solution:
Let $f(x) = \dfrac1{1+x^2}$. Jensen is not available: $f''(x) = \dfrac{6x^2 - 2}{(1+x^2)^3}$ is negative for $0 < x < 1/\sqrt3$, so $f$ is not convex on $(0, 3)$.

The expected equality point is $a = b = c = 1$. There $f(1) = \tfrac12$ and $f'(1) = -\tfrac{2x}{(1+x^2)^2}\big|_{x=1} = -\tfrac12$, so the tangent line is $\tfrac12 - \tfrac12(x - 1) = \tfrac{2 - x}{2}$. We claim $f(x) \ge \tfrac{2-x}{2}$ for all $x > 0$:

$$\frac1{1+x^2} - \frac{2-x}{2} = \frac{2 - (2-x)(1+x^2)}{2(1+x^2)} = \frac{x^3 - 2x^2 + x}{2(1+x^2)} = \frac{x(x-1)^2}{2(1+x^2)} \ge 0.$$

Adding the three inequalities for $a, b, c$:

$$\sum\frac1{1+a^2} \ge \frac{6 - (a+b+c)}{2} = \frac32,$$

with equality only for $a = b = c = 1$ (the factor $x(x-1)^2$ vanishes for positive $x$ only at $x = 1$).
blocks.title: The tangent line trick

blocks.body: Real numbers $a, b, c \in [0, 2]$ satisfy $a + b + c = 3$. Find the maximum of $a^3 + b^3 + c^3$.
blocks.solution:
By symmetry assume $a \ge b \ge c$. We claim $(2, 1, 0) \succ (a, b, c)$. Indeed $a \le 2$; $a + b = 3 - c \le 3 = 2 + 1$; and both lists sum to $3$.

The function $t^3$ is convex on $[0, 2]$ (its second derivative $6t$ is non-negative). By Karamata,

$$a^3 + b^3 + c^3 \le 2^3 + 1^3 + 0^3 = 9.$$

The value $9$ is attained at $(a,b,c) = (2, 1, 0)$, so the maximum is $9$. (By the same token, $(1,1,1)$ is majorized by every admissible list, so the minimum is $3$, at $a = b = c = 1$.)
blocks.title: Karamata with box constraints

blocks.body:
- The weights in Jensen must be non-negative. With $f(x) = x^2$, weights $w = (2, -1)$ (sum $1$) and points $x = (0, 1)$: the left side is $f(-1) = 1$, the right side is $2\cdot 0 - 1\cdot 1 = -1$, and the inequality fails.
- Convexity is a property on an interval. $1/x$ is convex on $(0, \infty)$ but not on $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and $f(x) = 1/(1+x^2)$ changes from concave to convex at $x = 1/\sqrt3$.
- $f'' > 0$ is sufficient for strict convexity but not necessary: $x^4$ is strictly convex although its second derivative vanishes at $0$.
- Karamata needs both lists sorted in the same (decreasing) order before comparing partial sums, and the totals must be equal.
- For a concave function every inequality above reverses; mixing the two directions is the most common slip.

Jensen's inequality (published by Johan Jensen in 1906) unifies [[amgm]] and the power means, and much of [[cauchy-schwarz]] and Hölder can also be derived from convexity. Majorization is the language behind Muirhead's inequality in [[symmetric-ineq]], and smoothing arguments are common in [[geo-inequalities]].

In probability, Jensen reads $f(\mathbb E X) \le \mathbb E f(X)$ for convex $f$ ([[random-variables]]); for instance $\mathbb E[X^2] \ge (\mathbb E X)^2$, which is the statement that variance is non-negative. In optimisation, convexity is what makes problems tractable: for a convex function on an interval every local minimum is a global minimum, and a strictly convex function has at most one minimum point. Constrained versions of this lead to [[lagrange-multipliers]].

1. Show that $x\ln x$ is convex on $(0, \infty)$, and deduce that $x^xy^y \ge \tfrac12$ for positive $x, y$ with $x + y = 1$.
2. Prove that among all convex $n$-gons inscribed in a fixed circle of radius $R$, the regular $n$-gon has the largest perimeter. (Write each side as $2R\sin(\theta_i/2)$ for central angles $\theta_i$.)
3. Show that $(n, 0, \dots, 0) \succ (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ for every list of non-negative reals with sum $n$, sorted decreasingly, and deduce a bound for $\sum x_i^4$.
4. Find all $x > 0$ for which $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{1+x^2}$ is concave.

sources.ref: Marshall, Olkin & Arnold, Inequalities: Theory of Majorization and Its Applications

blocks.body:
Many competition inequalities look like this: three non-negative variables $a, b, c$, a polynomial in them that does not change when the variables are permuted, and a claim that it is non-negative. AM–GM handles some of them, but others, such as

$$a^3 + b^3 + c^3 + 3abc \ge ab(a+b) + bc(b+c) + ca(c+a),$$

resist it, because the equality cases include not only $a = b = c$ but also points like $(1,1,0)$.

This page collects the standard tools for such inequalities: rewriting in terms of $p = a+b+c$, $q = ab+bc+ca$, $r = abc$; sum-of-squares (SOS) decompositions; Schur's inequality; Muirhead's inequality; and the $uvw$ (or $pqr$) method, which reduces a problem to the cases where two variables are equal or one is zero.

blocks.title: Symmetric polynomials and p, q, r
blocks.body:
A polynomial in $a, b, c$ is symmetric if it is unchanged by every permutation of the variables, and cyclic if it is unchanged by the cyclic shift $a \to b \to c \to a$. We write $\sum_{\text{cyc}} F(a,b,c) = F(a,b,c) + F(b,c,a) + F(c,a,b)$. For the sum over all six permutations we write out the terms; for example

$$\sum_{\text{sym}} a^2b = a^2b + a^2c + b^2a + b^2c + c^2a + c^2b.$$

The building blocks are the elementary symmetric polynomials, which are exactly the Vieta coefficients of the cubic with roots $a, b, c$ ([[polynomials-roots]]):

$$p = a+b+c,\qquad q = ab+bc+ca,\qquad r = abc,\qquad (x-a)(x-b)(x-c) = x^3 - px^2 + qx - r.$$

By the fundamental theorem on symmetric polynomials (proof omitted here), every symmetric polynomial in $a, b, c$ can be written as a polynomial in $p, q, r$. The most used conversions are

$$a^2+b^2+c^2 = p^2 - 2q,\qquad a^3+b^3+c^3 = p^3 - 3pq + 3r,$$

$$\sum_{\text{sym}} a^2b = pq - 3r,\qquad (a+b)(b+c)(c+a) = pq - r.$$

blocks.title: Sum of squares
blocks.body:
The most convincing proof that something is non-negative is to write it as a sum of squares, or of squares times obviously non-negative factors. Two identities to know by heart:

$$a^2+b^2+c^2 - ab - bc - ca = \tfrac12\big[(a-b)^2 + (b-c)^2 + (c-a)^2\big],$$

$$a^3+b^3+c^3 - 3abc = (a+b+c)\cdot\tfrac12\big[(a-b)^2 + (b-c)^2 + (c-a)^2\big].$$

The first gives $p^2 \ge 3q$ for all real $a, b, c$. The second shows $a^3+b^3+c^3 \ge 3abc$ whenever $a + b + c \ge 0$, a slightly stronger statement than AM–GM for three cubes.

Many symmetric inequalities can be brought to the SOS form $S_a(b-c)^2 + S_b(c-a)^2 + S_c(a-b)^2 \ge 0$ with coefficients $S_a, S_b, S_c$ depending on the variables; if the coefficients can be shown non-negative (or "non-negative enough"), the inequality follows.

blocks.title: Schur's inequality
blocks.body:
For $a, b, c \ge 0$ and $t > 0$,

$$\sum_{\text{cyc}} a^t(a-b)(a-c) \ge 0.$$

Equality holds if and only if $a = b = c$, or two of the variables are equal and the third is $0$.

For $t = 1$, expanding gives $a^3 + b^3 + c^3 + 3abc \ge \sum_{\text{sym}} a^2b$, which in terms of $p, q, r$ is

$$p^3 - 4pq + 9r \ge 0.$$

The expression is symmetric, so we may assume $a \ge b \ge c \ge 0$. Group the first two terms:

$$a^t(a-b)(a-c) + b^t(b-a)(b-c) = (a-b)\big[a^t(a-c) - b^t(b-c)\big].$$

Here $a - b \ge 0$, and $a^t \ge b^t \ge 0$ together with $a - c \ge b - c \ge 0$ give $a^t(a-c) \ge b^t(b-c)$. So this part is $\ge 0$. The third term is $c^t(c-a)(c-b) = c^t(a-c)(b-c) \ge 0$. Adding, the sum is $\ge 0$.

Equality. If $a > b$, then $a - c > 0$ and $a^t > b^t$, so $a^t(a-c) > b^t(a-c) \ge b^t(b-c)$ and the first part is strictly positive. Hence equality forces $a = b$. Then the sum reduces to the third term $c^t(a-c)^2$, which vanishes exactly when $c = 0$ or $c = a$. So equality holds precisely for $a = b = c$ and for $a = b$, $c = 0$ (up to order).

The $t = 1$ form: $a(a-b)(a-c) = a^3 - a^2b - a^2c + abc$, and summing cyclically gives $\sum a^3 - \sum_{\text{sym}}a^2b + 3abc$. Substituting the conversions above, $(p^3 - 3pq + 3r) - (pq - 3r) + 3r = p^3 - 4pq + 9r$.
blocks.title: Proof of Schur's inequality
Muirhead: comparing symmetric sums by their exponents
blocks.body:
For an exponent list $\alpha = (\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3)$ of non-negative reals, let $[\alpha]$ denote the sum of $a^{\alpha_1}b^{\alpha_2}c^{\alpha_3}$ over all $6$ orderings of the variables. For example

$$[2,0,0] = 2(a^2+b^2+c^2),\qquad [1,1,0] = 2(ab+bc+ca),\qquad [1,1,1] = 6abc.$$

Muirhead's inequality says that the more "spread out" the exponent list, the larger the sum. Spread is measured by majorization: for lists sorted decreasingly with the same total, $\alpha \succ \beta$ means $\alpha_1 \ge \beta_1$, $\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 \ge \beta_1 + \beta_2$, and so on, with equal totals. (The same notion drives Karamata's inequality on the [[convexity]] page.)

blocks.title: Muirhead's inequality
blocks.body:
Let $\alpha, \beta$ be exponent lists of non-negative reals of length $n$, sorted decreasingly, with $\alpha \succ \beta$. Then for all positive reals $x_1, \dots, x_n$

$$\sum_{\sigma} x_{\sigma(1)}^{\alpha_1}\cdots x_{\sigma(n)}^{\alpha_n} \;\ge\; \sum_{\sigma} x_{\sigma(1)}^{\beta_1}\cdots x_{\sigma(n)}^{\beta_n},$$

the sums running over all $n!$ permutations $\sigma$. If $\alpha \ne \beta$, equality holds only when all $x_i$ are equal.

We omit the proof; it can be done by obtaining $\beta$ from $\alpha$ through a finite chain of transfers, each moving some amount from a larger exponent to a smaller one, and checking each step with the two-variable inequality $x^{m+d}y^{m-d} + x^{m-d}y^{m+d} \ge x^{m+e}y^{m-e} + x^{m-e}y^{m+e}$ for $x, y > 0$ and $0 \le e \le d$ (see Hardy, Littlewood and Pólya). Note that AM–GM itself is the case $\alpha = (n, 0, \dots, 0)$, $\beta = (1, 1, \dots, 1)$.

blocks.title: Why Schur is not a consequence of Muirhead
blocks.body: In bracket notation the $t = 1$ Schur inequality is $[3,0,0] + [1,1,1] \ge 2\,[2,1,0]$. Muirhead gives $[3,0,0] \ge [2,1,0]$, but also $[2,1,0] \ge [1,1,1]$, which goes the wrong way for the second term. Schur balances a "spread" term against a "concentrated" one, and that is exactly why its equality cases include the boundary point $(1,1,0)$, where Muirhead-type inequalities are strict. Whenever an inequality has an equality case with a zero variable, AM–GM and Muirhead alone cannot prove it, and Schur (or the $uvw$ method below) is a natural candidate.

blocks.title: The uvw method: two equal or one zero
blocks.body:
Fix $p$ and $q$ and ask which values of $r$ are possible for non-negative reals $a, b, c$ with $a + b + c = p$ and $ab + bc + ca = q$. The variables are the roots of $x^3 - px^2 + qx - r$, i.e. the solutions of

$$g(x) = r,\qquad g(x) = x^3 - px^2 + qx.$$

Assume $p^2 > 3q$ (if $p^2 = 3q$ then $a = b = c$ and there is nothing to vary). Then $g'(x) = 3x^2 - 2px + q$ has two real zeros, so $g$ has a local maximum value $M$ and a local minimum value $m < M$. The horizontal line at height $r$ meets the graph in three points (counted with multiplicity) exactly when $m \le r \le M$, and at the two extremes it is tangent, which means a double root: two of $a, b, c$ are equal. Non-negativity adds one more condition: when $p, q, r \ge 0$, a negative $x$ makes every term of $x^3 - px^2 + qx - r$ non-positive and the first one negative, so there are no negative roots; thus the roots are non-negative precisely when $r \ge 0$.

Conclusion: for fixed $p, q$ the admissible values of $r$ form a closed interval $[\max(0, m), M]$, and at each endpoint either two variables are equal or one variable is $0$.

This gives the method. Write the inequality as $F(p, q, r) \ge 0$. If, for fixed $p$ and $q$, $F$ is linear in $r$ (or monotone, or concave), its minimum over the interval is at an endpoint, so it suffices to check the cases $b = c$ and $c = 0$. Schur's $p^3 - 4pq + 9r \ge 0$ is linear in $r$: with $c = 0$ it reads $a^3 + b^3 \ge ab(a+b)$, i.e. $(a+b)(a-b)^2 \ge 0$; with $b = c$ the original form $\sum a(a-b)(a-c)$ becomes $a(a-b)^2 \ge 0$. Both are clear, which proves Schur once more.
Prove that $a^3 + b^3 + c^3 \ge 3abc$ for all reals with $a + b + c \ge 0$, and find all equality cases.
blocks.solution:
By the second SOS identity,

$$a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc = \tfrac12(a+b+c)\big[(a-b)^2 + (b-c)^2 + (c-a)^2\big].$$

Both factors are non-negative when $a + b + c \ge 0$, so the difference is $\ge 0$. It vanishes exactly when $a + b + c = 0$ or $a = b = c$. For instance $(1, 2, -3)$ gives $1 + 8 - 27 = -18 = 3\cdot(-6)$, an equality case with unequal variables.
blocks.title: A factorisation

blocks.body: Prove that $a^4 + b^4 + c^4 \ge abc(a + b + c)$ for $a, b, c \ge 0$.
blocks.solution:
By Muirhead. The exponent lists are $(4, 0, 0)$ and $(2, 1, 1)$; we have $4 \ge 2$, $4 + 0 \ge 2 + 1$, and $4 = 4$, so $(4,0,0) \succ (2,1,1)$. Now $[4,0,0] = 2(a^4 + b^4 + c^4)$ and $[2,1,1] = 2(a^2bc + ab^2c + abc^2) = 2abc(a+b+c)$, and Muirhead gives the claim for positive variables (and by continuity for non-negative ones).

Directly. Apply $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \ge xy + yz + zx$ twice: first with $x, y, z = a^2, b^2, c^2$, then with $x, y, z = ab, bc, ca$:

$$a^4 + b^4 + c^4 \ge a^2b^2 + b^2c^2 + c^2a^2 \ge ab\cdot bc + bc\cdot ca + ca\cdot ab = abc(a + b + c).$$

Muirhead tells you the inequality is true before you find the trick; the direct proof is what you would usually write down.
blocks.title: Muirhead, and a direct proof

blocks.body:
Prove that for all $a, b, c \ge 0$,
$$4(a^3 + b^3 + c^3) + 15abc \ge (a + b + c)^3.$$
blocks.solution:
Convert: $4(p^3 - 3pq + 3r) + 15r - p^3 = 3p^3 - 12pq + 27r = 3\,(p^3 - 4pq + 9r)$.

So the inequality is exactly three times Schur's inequality with $t = 1$, and holds with the same equality cases: $a = b = c$, or two equal and the third zero. Check at $(1,1,0)$: $4\cdot 2 + 0 = 8 = 2^3$.

This is the main benefit of $p, q, r$: two inequalities that look unrelated in $a, b, c$ can turn out to be the same.
blocks.title: Translating to p, q, r

blocks.body:
Non-negative reals $a, b, c$ satisfy $a + b + c = 3$. Prove that
$$a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + abc \ge 4.$$
blocks.solution:
With $p = 3$ the left side is $9 - 2q + r$. Schur's inequality $p^3 - 4pq + 9r \ge 0$ becomes $27 - 12q + 9r \ge 0$, so

$$r \ge \frac{4q}{3} - 3.$$

Hence $9 - 2q + r \ge 9 - 2q + \tfrac{4q}{3} - 3 = 6 - \tfrac{2q}{3}$. Finally $q \le \tfrac{p^2}{3} = 3$ (from $p^2 \ge 3q$), so $6 - \tfrac{2q}{3} \ge 4$.

Equality needs $q = 3$, which forces $a = b = c = 1$, and indeed $1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4$. (At the Schur equality point $(\tfrac32, \tfrac32, 0)$ the left side is $\tfrac92$, so there the second step is strict.)
blocks.title: Schur with a constraint
Non-negative polynomials and sums of squares
blocks.body:
A sum of squares of real polynomials is non-negative everywhere. Is every polynomial that is non-negative everywhere a sum of squares of polynomials? In one variable the answer is yes (in fact two squares suffice). Hilbert showed in 1888 that in general the answer is no, and Motzkin later gave a famous explicit example,

$$M(x,y) = x^4y^2 + x^2y^4 - 3x^2y^2 + 1,$$

which is non-negative by AM–GM applied to $x^4y^2$, $x^2y^4$ and $1$ (their product is $x^6y^6$, so their mean is at least $x^2y^2$), and yet is not a sum of squares of polynomials. Hilbert's 17th problem (1900) asked whether every non-negative polynomial is at least a sum of squares of rational functions; Emil Artin proved in 1927 that it is. So "non-negative" and "sum of squares of polynomials" are genuinely different, and SOS proofs, while convincing when they exist, cannot always be found.

- Muirhead applies to full symmetric sums, not to cyclic ones. Since $(3,1,0) \succ (2,2,0)$, the symmetric inequality is true, but the cyclic version $a^3b + b^3c + c^3a \ge a^2b^2 + b^2c^2 + c^2a^2$ fails at $(a,b,c) = (0,1,2)$, where the left side is $2$ and the right side $4$.
- Schur's inequality needs non-negative variables: at $(a,b,c) = (-1, 0, 0)$ with $t = 1$ the sum is $-1$.
- "Without loss of generality $a \ge b \ge c$" is only valid for symmetric expressions. For cyclic ones you may only assume, say, that $a$ is the largest.
- The $uvw$ reduction needs the expression to be linear (or monotone, or concave) in $r$ for fixed $p, q$; it is not a licence to check only $b = c$ for an arbitrary inequality.
- Remember the boundary equality cases. An inequality that is tight at $(1,1,0)$ cannot be proved by a chain of AM–GM steps that are all strict there.

The $p, q, r$ substitution is [[polynomials-roots|Vieta's formulas]] read backwards, and the tools here sit on top of [[amgm]], [[cauchy-schwarz]] and [[convexity]] (majorization is common to Muirhead and Karamata). For triangle inequalities, the Ravi substitution $a = y + z$, $b = z + x$, $c = x + y$ with $x, y, z > 0$ turns a statement about the sides of a triangle into a symmetric inequality in three positive variables, which links this page to [[geo-inequalities]].

The question of when a non-negative polynomial is a sum of squares, behind Hilbert's 17th problem, is today a working tool: searching for SOS certificates is a standard computational method for proving polynomial inequalities.

1. Express $a^4 + b^4 + c^4$ in terms of $p, q, r$.
2. Show that Schur's inequality with $t = 2$ is equivalent to $a^4 + b^4 + c^4 + abc(a+b+c) \ge \sum_{\text{sym}} a^3b$.
3. Arrange the exponent lists $(4,0,0)$, $(3,1,0)$, $(2,2,0)$, $(2,1,1)$ in a chain under majorization and write down the resulting inequalities.
4. Prove that $a^3b + b^3c + c^3a \ge abc(a + b + c)$ for positive $a, b, c$.

sources.ref: Pham Kim Hung, Secrets in Inequalities

blocks.body:
A functional equation asks for every function satisfying some identity, for example all $f : \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ with $f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y)$ for all real $x, y$. The unknown is a whole function, so the usual algebra of "isolate $x$" does not apply. Instead one feeds the identity well-chosen inputs, extracts properties of $f$ (its value at $0$, oddness, injectivity, its values on the rationals), and finally pins $f$ down.

This page explains the standard moves through the most important example, Cauchy's equation, including the surprising fact that without some regularity condition it has solutions that are not of the form $cx$.

blocks.title: What solving means
blocks.body:
"Find all functions" has two halves. First, necessity: assuming $f$ satisfies the equation, show that $f$ must be one of a list of candidates. Second, sufficiency: check that every candidate really satisfies the equation. Skipping the second half is a classic way to lose points, because the necessity argument often uses only some of the information.

The basic toolkit:

- Special values: put $x = 0$, $y = 0$, $x = y$, $y = -x$, or $y = 1$ to learn $f(0)$, parity, or a recursion.
- Swapping: if the equation is not symmetric in $x$ and $y$, swap them and compare the two versions.
- Injectivity and surjectivity: if $f(a) = f(b)$ forces $a = b$, you can cancel $f$; if every real is a value of $f$, you can substitute $f(y)$ for an arbitrary real.
- Reduction: subtract a guessed particular solution and see whether the remainder satisfies a simpler, known equation.
- Regularity: once $f$ is known on the rationals, a hypothesis such as continuity or monotonicity spreads the formula to all reals.

blocks.title: Cauchy's functional equation
blocks.body:
Let $f : \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ satisfy $f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y)$ for all real $x, y$, and put $c = f(1)$. Then $f(q) = cq$ for every rational $q$. If in addition $f$ is monotone, or continuous, then $f(x) = cx$ for every real $x$:

$$f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y),\ f \text{ monotone} \Rightarrow f(x)=cx.$$

Step 1 (integers). Putting $x = y = 0$ gives $f(0) = 2f(0)$, so $f(0) = 0$. Putting $y = -x$ gives $f(x) + f(-x) = f(0) = 0$, so $f$ is odd. By induction on $n$, $f(nx) = f((n-1)x) + f(x) = nf(x)$ for every positive integer $n$, and by oddness for every integer $n$.

Step 2 (rationals). Let $q = m/n$ with integers $m$ and $n \ge 1$. By step 1, $nf(m/n) = f(m) = mf(1) = mc$, so $f(q) = cq$.

Step 3 (monotone). Suppose $f$ is non-decreasing (the non-increasing case is the same with inequalities reversed). Let $x$ be real and $r < x < s$ rationals. Then $cr = f(r) \le f(x) \le f(s) = cs$. Rationals $r$ and $s$ can be chosen as close to $x$ as we like, so both $cr$ and $cs$ come arbitrarily close to $cx$, and $f(x) = cx$.

Step 3' (continuous). Choose rationals $q_k \to x$ (decimal truncations, say). By continuity $f(x) = \lim f(q_k) = \lim cq_k = cx$.
blocks.title: Proof
Weaker regularity is enough, and none is not
blocks.body:
The regularity hypothesis can be weakened a lot. Continuity at a single point $x_0$ already suffices: additivity gives $f(x + h) - f(x) = f(x_0 + h) - f(x_0)$ for every $x$, so continuity at $x_0$ implies continuity everywhere. It is also known (proof omitted here) that an additive function bounded above on some interval of positive length, or merely measurable, is linear.

But some hypothesis is necessary. View $\mathbb R$ as a vector space over the field $\mathbb Q$ of rationals ([[vector-spaces]]). Using the axiom of choice one can find a basis of this space, called a Hamel basis after Georg Hamel, who used one in 1905 to construct exactly such functions. Every real number is then uniquely a finite combination $x = q_1b_1 + \cdots + q_kb_k$ of basis elements with rational coefficients. Choose two different basis elements $b$ and $b'$, and let $f(x)$ be the coefficient of $b$ in the expansion of $x$; so $f(b) = 1$ and $f$ vanishes on every other basis element, $b'$ included. This $f$ is additive, since coefficients add. But it is not of the form $cx$: $f(b) = 1$ forces $c = 1/b$, while $f(b') = 0$ forces $c = 0$.

Such wild solutions are strange: one can show that the graph of an additive function that is not linear is dense in the plane, so it is not monotone on any interval, not continuous at any point, and not bounded on any interval. That is why every competition problem leading to Cauchy's equation must either assume regularity or contain enough information to prove it, as in Example 4.

blocks.title: Relatives of Cauchy's equation
blocks.body:
Three cousins reduce to Cauchy's equation by a change of variables. For continuous $f$:

1. $f(x + y) = f(x)f(y)$ on $\mathbb R$: either $f \equiv 0$ or $f(x) = a^x$ for some $a > 0$.
2. $f(xy) = f(x) + f(y)$ on $(0, \infty)$: $f(x) = c\ln x$.
3. $f(xy) = f(x)f(y)$ on $(0, \infty)$: either $f \equiv 0$ or $f(x) = x^c$.

For the first: $f(x) = f(x/2)^2 \ge 0$. If $f(x_0) = 0$ for some $x_0$ then $f(x) = f(x_0)f(x - x_0) = 0$ for every $x$. Otherwise $f > 0$ and $g = \ln f$ is continuous and additive, so $g(x) = cx$ and $f(x) = e^{cx} = a^x$ with $a = e^c$. For the second, $g(u) = f(e^u)$ is additive. The third combines both ideas (see [[exp-log]]).
Find all $f : \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ with $f(x) + 2f(1 - x) = x^2$ for all real $x$.
blocks.solution:
Replace $x$ by $1 - x$ (allowed, since the identity holds for every real number): $f(1 - x) + 2f(x) = (1-x)^2$.

For each fixed $x$ we now have two linear equations in the two unknowns $u = f(x)$ and $v = f(1-x)$:

$$u + 2v = x^2,\qquad 2u + v = (1-x)^2.$$

Doubling the second and subtracting the first gives $3u = 2(1-x)^2 - x^2$, so

$$f(x) = \frac{2(1-x)^2 - x^2}{3} = \frac{x^2 - 4x + 2}{3}.$$

Check: $f(1-x) = \tfrac{(1-x)^2 - 4(1-x) + 2}{3} = \tfrac{x^2 + 2x - 1}{3}$, and $f(x) + 2f(1-x) = \tfrac{x^2 - 4x + 2 + 2x^2 + 4x - 2}{3} = x^2$. So this is the unique solution.
blocks.title: Solving a linear system of values

blocks.body: Find all continuous $f : \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ with $f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y) + 2xy$ for all real $x, y$.
blocks.solution:
The term $2xy$ is what $(x+y)^2 - x^2 - y^2$ produces, which suggests subtracting $x^2$. Let $g(x) = f(x) - x^2$. Then

$$g(x+y) = f(x) + f(y) + 2xy - (x+y)^2 = \big(f(x) - x^2\big) + \big(f(y) - y^2\big) = g(x) + g(y).$$

So $g$ is additive and continuous, hence $g(x) = cx$ by Cauchy's theorem, and $f(x) = x^2 + cx$.

Check: $(x+y)^2 + c(x+y) = (x^2 + cx) + (y^2 + cy) + 2xy$. So the solutions are $f(x) = x^2 + cx$ for any real constant $c$.
blocks.title: Reducing to Cauchy

blocks.body:
Find all monotone $f : \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ such that
$$f(x + f(y)) = f(x) + y\qquad\text{for all real } x, y.$$
blocks.solution:
Put $x = 0$ and write $a = f(0)$: $f(f(y)) = a + y$. The right side takes every real value exactly once as $y$ varies, so $f$ is surjective, and if $f(y_1) = f(y_2)$ then $a + y_1 = a + y_2$, so $f$ is injective.

Put $y = 0$: $f(x + a) = f(x)$ for all $x$. By injectivity $x + a = x$, so $a = 0$. Thus $f(f(y)) = y$ for every $y$: $f$ is an involution.

Now take any reals $x$ and $z$, and use the equation with $y = f(z)$, so that $f(y) = f(f(z)) = z$:

$$f(x + z) = f(x) + f(z).$$

So $f$ is additive and, being monotone, $f(x) = cx$. Then $f(f(x)) = c^2x = x$ forces $c = \pm1$.

Check: for $f(x) = x$ both sides equal $x + y$; for $f(x) = -x$ the left side is $-(x - y) = y - x$ and the right side is $-x + y$. Both work, so the answer is $f(x) = x$ and $f(x) = -x$.

Without monotonicity the argument still shows that $f$ must be an additive involution, and there are wild additive involutions (built from a Hamel basis, as above), so the hypothesis cannot simply be dropped.
blocks.title: Injectivity and an involution

blocks.body:
Find all $f : \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ that are both additive and multiplicative:
$$f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y),\qquad f(xy) = f(x)f(y)\qquad\text{for all real } x, y.$$
No continuity is assumed.
blocks.solution:
The point is that multiplicativity supplies the missing regularity.

For $t \ge 0$, $f(t) = f(\sqrt t\cdot\sqrt t) = f(\sqrt t)^2 \ge 0$. Hence if $x \le y$, then $f(y) - f(x) = f(y - x) \ge 0$ (additivity gives $f(y) = f(x) + f(y-x)$). So $f$ is non-decreasing.

By Cauchy's theorem $f(x) = cx$ with $c = f(1)$. Multiplicativity then gives $cxy = c^2xy$ for all $x, y$, so $c^2 = c$, i.e. $c = 0$ or $c = 1$.

Both $f \equiv 0$ and $f(x) = x$ satisfy the two equations, so these are the only solutions. (In the language of algebra: the only ring homomorphism from $\mathbb R$ to itself sending $1$ to $1$ is the identity.)
blocks.title: Regularity for free

blocks.body:
- Forgetting to verify. Necessity arguments often throw information away; always substitute the candidates back.
- The pointwise trap. From $f(x)^2 = x^2$ for all $x$ you may only conclude that for each $x$, $f(x) = x$ or $f(x) = -x$. The choice can change from point to point (for example $f(x) = |x|$), so "$f(x) = x$ for all $x$ or $f(x) = -x$ for all $x$" needs a further argument.
- Assuming continuity, differentiability or a polynomial form that the problem does not give. Over the reals, Cauchy's equation alone does not force linearity.
- Dividing by $f(x)$ without checking that it is nonzero, or plugging in a value outside the domain (for equations on $(0,\infty)$ or $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$).
- Confusing "$f$ is injective" with "$f$ has an inverse on all of $\mathbb R$": the latter also needs surjectivity.

Additive functions are exactly the $\mathbb Q$-linear maps $\mathbb R \to \mathbb R$, so Cauchy's equation is a question in [[linear-maps|linear algebra]] over $\mathbb Q$, and the wild solutions exist because of [[basis-dimension|bases]] of an infinite-dimensional space. The step from rationals to reals is the density of $\mathbb Q$ in [[real-numbers|the real line]] combined with [[continuity]] or monotonicity. The exponential relatives tie in with [[exp-log]] and with the simplest differential equations ([[ode-first]]: $f' = cf$ is the differentiable version of $f(x+y) = f(x)f(y)$).

For functions on the integers or the positive integers, the same moves are used, but induction replaces density and divisibility arguments appear; see [[integer-functional-eq]].
